analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 95% tax on large corporations' profits above their pre-2020 baseline through 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 with 4 cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new tax on very large corporations — those with at least $500 million in average annual gross receipts — equal to 95% of profits that exceed the company's inflation-adjusted average profit from 2015 through 2019. The tax would apply to taxable years after 2023 and expire after 2026. It also tightens rules that determine what counts as profit, including limiting the deductibility of executive pay and cracking down on offshore profit-shifting and accelerated depreciation. The bill never got any action beyond being referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury, and by extension general taxpayers, would receive the revenue from the new excess-profits tax. Ordinary people benefit only to the extent the revenue is used for public purposes; the bill itself does not direct the money to any specific program.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a tax equal to 95% of a large corporation's profits above its inflation-adjusted average annual profit for 2015-2019, so wartime or post-pandemic profit windfalls above the old baseline are taxed at the highest rate since World War II excess-profits taxes.
Applies only to corporations with average annual gross receipts of at least $500 million, leaving smaller businesses and S corporations unaffected.

Broadens what counts as taxable profit: it eliminates deductions that let multinationals reduce US tax on offshore income (FDII and GILTI, including the 'tangible income return' exemption), requires slower depreciation schedules, applies the research-expense amortization rules retroactively to 2021 and earlier, and extends the $1 million cap on deducting executive compensation to essentially all high-paid employees of covered companies, not just the top officers.
Runs through the end of 2026, making it a temporary measure rather than a permanent change to corporate tax law.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — roughly the biggest 1% or so of companies by revenue — pay the new tax, either out of profit margins (reducing shareholder returns) or by passing costs to consumers through prices. Highly paid employees of those companies lose a tax break on compensation above $1 million.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets no spending purpose: it raises revenue for the Treasury generally, so a supporter cannot point to a specific benefit — lower deficits, a dividend, or a program — that the tax delivers.

Taxing 95% of profits above a pre-2020 baseline gives companies that crossed the line after 2019 a marginal tax rate of 95% on further growth, which could discourage expansion, price-cutting, or investment during the covered years — the same incentive problem that historically led Congress to let earlier excess-profits taxes lapse.

The 2015-2019 baseline can be arbitrary: a company that was unprofitable or small before 2020 (or grew because consumers chose it) pays the tax on genuine new growth, while one whose profits simply stayed flat pays nothing.
The definition of 'excess profits' requires technical adjustments to offshore income, depreciation, and pay-cap rules that would be difficult to administer and could be avoided with restructuring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax would raise substantial money from a small number of very profitable companies, and the windfall-profits framing has an intuitive fairness appeal: profits far above a company's own recent history are treated as abnormal. But the design is blunt. A permanent-style penalty rate of 95% on profits above a fixed baseline, with no specified use for the money and real risk of discouraging growth or raising consumer prices, made the bill as much a statement as a workable tax policy. Honest supporters would acknowledge it needed a spending purpose and a less cliff-like structure to become serious legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Jamaal Bowman introduced the bill on June 21, 2024, joined by Representatives Jayapal, Schakowsky, and Tlaib.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is where all tax legislation must start.
No further action appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor consideration before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their shareholders, since no excess-profits tax or restrictions on offshore-profit deductions or executive pay deductions took effect. The Ways and Means Committee leadership was also spared having to act on a proposal its majority did not support.

for.name: Rep. Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on June 21, 2024.

for.name: Reps. Pramila Jayapal, Jan Schakowsky, and Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced; no others signed on during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never took the bill up; no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Large corporations with $500M+ annual gross receipts
industries.note: These companies would owe 95% of profits above their inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average through 2026, on top of regular taxes. Because the bill raises general revenue without earmarking it, the industry's gain from blocking it is simply keeping the money; ordinary people lost only a potential source of federal funds.

industries.industry: Executives and highly paid employees at large companies
industries.note: The bill would extend the $1 million cap on tax-deductible executive pay to essentially all employees of covered companies, ending a deduction worth millions a year in taxes for some firms.

The bill eliminates deductions that reduce US tax on foreign-derived and global intangible income and removes the 'tangible income return' exemption, so income shifted to low-tax jurisdictions would face the excess-profits tax. This raises US revenue but adds to the bill's complexity.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts, regulated investment companies, and S corporations
industries.note: These business forms are expressly exempt from the tax, so similarly sized firms organized as REITs or partnerships would avoid it while their corporate competitors paid.
